# Introduction

## Setting the scene

Singapore builds MRT stations years before the surrounding towns fill up. Hume station sat as a finished shell for a decade, and Buangkok and Woodleigh stayed shut when the North-East Line opened in 2003 because SBS Transit judged their expected ridership too low to cover operating costs. Two new lines are now under construction. The **Jurong Region Line (JRL)** has 24 stations opening in three stages from mid-2028 to 2029. **Cross Island Line Phase 1 (CRL1)** has 12 stations from Aviation Park to Bright Hill and is due in 2030. Planners therefore need a defensible way to estimate how many people each new station will attract and which existing stations will lose riders to them.

## Research question and objectives

> **Research question:** Can a probabilistic spatial interaction model calibrated on observed tap-in data reproduce station-level ridership on Singapore's current rail network well enough to estimate demand at the 29 new JRL/CRL1 stations, and to show how those stations reshape the market areas of existing stations?

| # | Objective (handout) | Where it is addressed |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction model for station-level ridership | @sec-sim (flow model) and @sec-huff (Huff model) |
| O2 | Predict ridership of the proposed JRL and CRL1 stations | @sec-scenario |
| O3 | Evaluate the impact of the new stations on existing stations | @sec-impact and @sec-market |

The eight handout tasks map onto the report as follows: the two spatial interaction data frames, the origin data frame and the destination data frame (Tasks 1–3) are built in @sec-sidf; calibration and estimation (Tasks 4–6) are in @sec-sim and @sec-huff; prediction and impact (Tasks 7–8) are in @sec-scenario to @sec-market.

## Analytical framework

The study uses two complementary probabilistic spatial interaction models from the course.

1. **Station-to-station spatial interaction models (SIM, Chapter 16).** Poisson gravity models (unconstrained, origin-, destination- and doubly-constrained) are calibrated on observed MRT/LRT origin–destination flows. They reveal how strongly trip volumes decay with distance and which constraint structure fits the data.
2. **Huff model (Chapter 18, `MCI` package).** Each resident subzone is treated as a market and each station as a competing "store". The probability that residents of subzone *i* board at station *j* is

$$P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, f(d_{ij})}{\sum_{k} A_k \, f(d_{ik})}, \qquad A_j = n^{\gamma}_{j}\,e^{\delta \cdot LRT_j}$$

where $f(d_{ij})$ is a distance-decay function (power or exponential; @sec-huff selects between them), $n_j$ is the number of rail lines serving the station and $LRT_j$ flags LRT-only stations. Expected boardings at station *j* are $\hat{B}_j = k\sum_i P_{ij}\,Pop_i$, where $k$ is a system trip rate. Parameters $\gamma$, $\delta$ and $\lambda$ are calibrated against observed **weekday morning-peak tap-ins**, and the fitted model is then re-run with the new stations added.

The Huff model is the main prediction engine because it can price in a station that has no ridership history yet: all it needs is the station's location and attributes. The SIM explains the flow structure that the Huff model abstracts away.

## Key assumptions and methodological decisions

| Decision | Choice made | Reason | Alternative tested or rejected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dependent variable | Weekday 06:00–09:59 tap-ins | Home-based boardings match a residential demand model | Total daily ridership, which mixes in destination demand |
| Origins | 286 populated subzones with HDB-weighted centroids | Places demand where residents actually live | Plain polygon centroids |
| Station coordinates | SVY21 `X`/`Y`, falling back to lat/long | Lat/long misplaces Rochor by about 350 m; confirmed against LTA station exits (@sec-quality) | Lat/long throughout |
| Destination attractors (MCI) | Master Plan job/education floor area | Captures *planned* development around new stations | OSM POIs, which record only what exists today |
| Future stations | 29 new + 7 upgraded interchanges (official JRL/CRL1 list) | The URA layer mixes in 60+ non-JRL/CRL1 names | Naive name anti-join (98 "new" stations) |
| Attraction $A_j$ | Lines served and LRT penalty | Best fit per parameter; forecastable for new stations | Closeness centrality; HDB within 800 m |
| Distance decay | Exponential, calibrated $\lambda$ | Better fit; no unrealistic long tail | Power function (Chapter 18 default) |
| Calibration | RMSE minimised by `optim()`, 5-fold cross-validation | Unbounded search; out-of-sample check | Coarse fixed grid |
| Total demand | Fixed trip rate $k$ | Isolates the spatial reallocation effect | Tengah build-out sensitivity adds residents |
| Benchmarks | Nearest station; default Huff | The calibrated model must beat simple rules | – |

# Packages

The packages are loaded with `pacman::p_load()`, which installs any that are missing so the report renders end to end on a fresh machine.

| Package | Role in this study |
|---|---|
| `sf` | Import, project, join and measure geospatial data |
| `tidyverse` | Data wrangling (`dplyr`, `tidyr`, `stringr`) and graphics (`ggplot2`) |
| `igraph` | Build the rail network graph; network distances and centrality |
| `MCI` | Huff market shares (`huff.shares()`) and station totals (`shares.total()`) |
| `performance` | Model comparison for the Poisson SIMs (`compare_performance()`) |
| `spdep` | Spatial weights, global and local Moran's I on model residuals |
| `SpatialAcc` | KD2SFCA accessibility (value-added analysis) |
| `tmap` | Cartographic-quality thematic maps |
| `ggpubr`, `ggstatsplot` | Multi-panel diagnostics and observed-vs-predicted plots |
| `knitr` | Report tables |

```{r}
#| label: setup
pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse, igraph, MCI, SpatialAcc, spdep,
               tmap, performance, ggpubr, ggstatsplot, ggrepel, knitr, scales)

sf_use_s2(FALSE)           # planar geometry: all analysis is in SVY21 (EPSG:3414)
tmap_mode("plot")
set.seed(626)

fmt <- function(x, d = 0) scales::comma(x, accuracy = 10^-d)

# Interactive maps: render a tmap object as a Leaflet widget with real basemaps
# Esri tiles (as used in the course notes) need no API key; CARTO tiles now do.
basemaps <- tm_basemap(c("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldImagery"))
# Notes from testing: tm_symbols() draws oversized legend glyphs in view mode, so tm_dots()
# is used; set_view opens every map on Singapore instead of the whole Johor-Riau region.
as_leaflet <- function(m) {
  widget <- tmap_leaflet(basemaps + m + tm_view(set_view = c(103.82, 1.355, 11)),
                         mode = "view")   # returned invisibly by tmap
  widget
}
# Context layer shared by the interactive maps: the full May 2022 network in light grey
network_context <- function() tm_shape(net_base_sf) + tm_lines(col = "grey55", lwd = 1.2, col_alpha = 0.8)

# Display rule for subzone maps: hide subzones that are essentially unpopulated
# (< 100 residents or < 100 residents per km2, e.g. Murai military training area,
# 640 residents over 69 km2), so that large empty polygons do not dominate the map.
populated_for_map <- function(x) {
  x %>% filter(pop >= 100, pop / (as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6) >= 100)
}
pct <- function(x, d = 1) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 10^-d)
```

# Data

## Data sources

| Data set | Source | Format | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Train Stations, May 2022 | LTA DataMall (public mirror) | CSV | Observed tap-ins and station-to-station flows |
| Train station coordinates | LTA (public mirror) | CSV | Existing station locations and codes |
| Master Plan 2025 Rail Station layer | URA via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Locations of future stations |
| Planned JRL/CRL1 station list | Compiled from LTA announcements | CSV | Official station codes, branches and interchanges |
| Resident population by subzone, Census 2020 | SingStat via data.gov.sg | CSV | Origin market potential |
| Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (no sea) | URA via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Spatial origins |
| HDB Existing Building | HDB via data.gov.sg | GeoJSON | Residential intensity (population-weighted centroids, station catchments) |
| Master Plan 2019 Land Use layer | URA, via the `home2park` R package's GitHub mirror | GeoJSON (cleaned) | Job, education and residential floor area around each station |
| Bus Stop Location (Sep 2026) | LTA DataMall, static geospatial dataset | ESRI shapefile | Feeder-bus intensity around each station |
| Train Station Exit Point (Jul 2026) | LTA DataMall, static geospatial dataset | ESRI shapefile | Independent check of station coordinates |
| OpenStreetMap points of interest (extract of 2026-11-08) | Geofabrik `malaysia-singapore-brunei-latest-free.shp.zip`, clipped to Singapore | GeoPackage (clipped) | Retail, food, education, health and leisure destinations around each station |
| Annual public transport ridership 1995–2024 | LTA via data.gov.sg | CSV | System-level context |

LTA DataMall only serves the three most recent months of OD data, so May 2022 is the most recent month for which a complete public archive was available. It is a post-COVID month with the TEL stage 3 and 4 stations not yet open, which defines the baseline network for this study.

The bus-stop and station-exit shapefiles are used exactly as downloaded from LTA DataMall. The land-use layer comes from a public GitHub mirror of URA's Master Plan 2019 release; only the land-use type and gross plot ratio (GPR) of business, commercial, white, hotel, health, educational and residential parcels are kept. The OpenStreetMap extract covers Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei; its point and polygon POI layers are clipped to Singapore's subzone boundary (@sec-quality) and saved as a single GeoPackage.

The planned-station list (`planned_stations_jrl_crl.csv`) records the 24 JRL and 12 CRL1 station codes, their branch and sequence along the line, the matching name in the URA layer, and the existing station each interchange connects to. It was compiled from LTA's published station lists because the URA layer carries names but no line, code or opening date.

## Import

```{r}
#| label: import
od_raw          <- read_csv("data/aspatial/mrt_od_202205.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
station_points  <- read_csv("data/aspatial/mrt_station_points.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
planned         <- read_csv("data/aspatial/planned_stations_jrl_crl.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pop_raw         <- read_csv("data/aspatial/resident_population_subzone_2020.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ridership_trend <- read_csv("data/aspatial/public_transport_ridership_1995_2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

rail_2025 <- st_read("data/geospatial/rail_station_layer_2025.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
subzones  <- st_read("data/geospatial/MP19_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
hdb       <- st_read("data/geospatial/HDBExistingBuilding.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
landuse   <- st_read("data/geospatial/mp19_landuse_attractors.geojson", quiet = TRUE)
bus_stops <- st_read("data/geospatial/BusStop.shp", quiet = TRUE)
stn_exits <- st_read("data/geospatial/Train_Station_Exit_Layer.shp", quiet = TRUE)
osm_poi   <- st_read("data/geospatial/osm_pois_sg.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

tibble(layer = c("rail_2025", "subzones", "hdb", "landuse", "bus_stops", "stn_exits", "osm_poi"),
       features = c(nrow(rail_2025), nrow(subzones), nrow(hdb), nrow(landuse), nrow(bus_stops),
                    nrow(stn_exits), nrow(osm_poi)),
       crs = c(st_crs(rail_2025)$input, st_crs(subzones)$input, st_crs(hdb)$input,
               st_crs(landuse)$input, st_crs(bus_stops)$input, st_crs(stn_exits)$input,
               st_crs(osm_poi)$input),
       epsg = c(st_crs(rail_2025)$epsg, st_crs(subzones)$epsg, st_crs(hdb)$epsg,
                st_crs(landuse)$epsg, st_crs(bus_stops)$epsg, st_crs(stn_exits)$epsg,
                st_crs(osm_poi)$epsg))
```

**Mine 0:** the layers arrive in three different reference systems. The URA and HDB layers are in WGS84 (geographic degrees); the land-use and OSM files were already projected to EPSG:3414 when they were prepared. The two LTA shapefiles declare a custom "SVY21" projection with no EPSG code, so `st_crs()$epsg` is `NA`. Its parameters (false easting 28,001.642 m, false northing 38,744.572 m, origin at 1.3667°N, 103.8333°E) are those of SVY21 / Singapore TM. The correct fix is therefore to *assign* EPSG:3414 with `st_set_crs()`; reprojecting with `st_transform()` would move every stop by the difference between two definitions of the same grid.  Distances and buffers must be computed in metres, so every layer is projected to **SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414)** before any measurement. `st_make_valid()` repairs the six self-intersecting subzone polygons found by `st_is_valid()` and the few slivers in the simplified land-use layer, so that spatial joins and intersections do not fail or silently drop features.

```{r}
#| label: project
subzones <- subzones %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
hdb      <- hdb %>% st_transform(3414)
rail_2025 <- rail_2025 %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
landuse  <- landuse %>% st_transform(3414) %>% st_make_valid()
# LTA shapefiles carry a custom "SVY21" definition with no EPSG code. Its parameters are
# those of SVY21 / Singapore TM, so the code is *assigned* (st_set_crs), not reprojected.
bus_stops <- bus_stops %>% st_set_crs(3414)
stn_exits <- stn_exits %>% st_set_crs(3414)
osm_poi   <- osm_poi %>% st_transform(3414)
```

The annual series (@fig-trend) puts the study month in context. May 2022 sits in the recovery phase after the 2020 collapse, so absolute volumes are below the 2019 peak. Because the Huff model allocates a fixed demand total across stations, this mostly affects the scale of predictions, not the relative ranking of stations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trend
#| fig-cap: "Average daily rail ridership, 1995–2024. The dashed line marks the OD study month (May 2022)."
#| fig-height: 4
ridership_trend %>%
  filter(mode %in% c("MRT", "LRT")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, ridership, colour = mode)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2022, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(MRT = "#176b87", LRT = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average daily ridership", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Data preparation and quality assessment {#sec-quality}

The handout warns that "all data are like vast grassland full of land mines". This section documents each mine found and how it was cleared.

## Origin–destination records

```{r}
#| label: od-quality
od_raw %>%
  summarise(rows = n(),
            months = n_distinct(YEAR_MONTH),
            pt_types = n_distinct(PT_TYPE),
            hours = str_c(min(TIME_PER_HOUR), "–", max(TIME_PER_HOUR)),
            station_codes = n_distinct(c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DESTINATION_PT_CODE)),
            missing_values = sum(is.na(TOTAL_TRIPS)),
            negative_trips = sum(TOTAL_TRIPS < 0),
            total_trips = sum(TOTAL_TRIPS))
```

The OD file is internally clean: one month, train trips only, no missing or negative counts. Each record is a tap-in/tap-out pair aggregated by hour and day type. **Mine 1:** these are *tap-in to tap-out* journeys, so transfers inside the paid area are invisible. A trip from an LRT station to the CBD is recorded once, at its LRT origin. Tap-ins are therefore a clean measure of where people *enter* the network, which is exactly what a residential catchment model predicts.

## Existing stations

```{r}
#| label: station-xy-check
xy_missing <- station_points %>% filter(is.na(X) | is.na(Y))

xy_check <- station_points %>%
  filter(!is.na(X)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3414) %>%
  mutate(dev_m = sqrt((st_coordinates(.)[, 1] - X)^2 + (st_coordinates(.)[, 2] - Y)^2))

xy_missing %>% select(STN_NAME, STN_NO, X, Y, Latitude, Longitude)
summary(xy_check$dev_m)

# Which coordinate is right where the two disagree? Test both against the URA station footprints.
ura_footprint <- rail_2025 %>% mutate(name = str_squish(NAME))
fp_dist <- function(pt, nm) min(as.numeric(st_distance(pt, ura_footprint[ura_footprint$name == nm, ])))

xy_disagree <- xy_check %>%
  filter(dev_m > 50) %>%
  mutate(name = str_remove(STN_NAME, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$"))

xy_disagree %>%
  mutate(latlon_to_footprint_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) fp_dist(st_geometry(xy_disagree)[i], name[i])),
         xy_to_footprint_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i)
           fp_dist(st_sfc(st_point(c(X[i], Y[i])), crs = 3414), name[i]))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(STN_NAME, STN_NO, dev_m = round(dev_m),
            latlon_to_footprint_m = round(latlon_to_footprint_m),
            xy_to_footprint_m = round(xy_to_footprint_m))
```

**Mine 2:** the station file stores each location twice, as SVY21 `X`/`Y` and as WGS84 latitude/longitude, and the two disagree.

- The five TEL stage 2 stations have **no `X`/`Y`** at all. Building the layer from `X`/`Y` alone would drop them or fail.
- For the other 162 stations, projected latitude/longitude lies within a median of `r fmt(median(xy_check$dev_m), 1)` m of `X`/`Y`, but three stations disagree by more than 100 m. Testing both points against the URA station footprints settles which is right. For **Rochor**, the latitude/longitude is about 350 m away from the station while `X`/`Y` falls inside its footprint. For Little India and Outram Park, both points fall inside the large multi-line footprints.

The rule adopted is therefore: **use the native SVY21 `X`/`Y` where present, and projected latitude/longitude only for the five stations without it**. The original version of this analysis used latitude/longitude throughout and so misplaced Rochor.

```{r}
#| label: station-operational
od_codes <- unique(c(od_raw$ORIGIN_PT_CODE, od_raw$DESTINATION_PT_CODE))

non_operational <- tribble(
  ~stn_code, ~station, ~status_may_2022,
  "BP14", "Ten Mile Junction", "Bukit Panjang LRT station closed in January 2019",
  "CC18", "Bukit Brown",       "Shell station built in 2009 but never opened",
  "PW2",  "Teck Lee",          "Punggol LRT station opened only in August 2024")

stopifnot(all(non_operational$stn_code %in% setdiff(station_points$STN_NO, od_codes)))
non_operational
```

**Mine 3:** three codes in the station file never appear in the OD data. They are not join errors. They are stations that carried no passengers in May 2022, and one of them, **Bukit Brown, is itself a ghost station**. Keeping them would add three "observed zero" stations to the calibration and bias the model downwards, so they are removed. All remaining 164 station codes match the OD codes exactly, including the combined interchange codes such as `NS24/NE6/CC1`.

```{r}
#| label: stations-existing
latlon_svy21 <- station_points %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(3414) %>% st_coordinates()

stations <- station_points %>%
  mutate(x = coalesce(X, latlon_svy21[, 1]), y = coalesce(Y, latlon_svy21[, 2])) %>%
  filter(!STN_NO %in% non_operational$stn_code) %>%
  transmute(stn_code = STN_NO,
            stn_name = str_squish(str_remove(STN_NAME, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$")),
            x, y) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 3414)

nrow(stations)
```

The LTA station-exit layer gives an independent check of the adopted coordinates: every station point should lie within a short walk of its own exits.

```{r}
#| label: station-exit-check
exits_named <- stn_exits %>%
  mutate(stn_name = str_squish(str_remove(stn_name, " (MRT|LRT) STATION$")))

exit_check <- stations %>%
  mutate(nearest_own_exit_m = map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) {
    own <- exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == stn_name[i], ]
    if (nrow(own) == 0) NA_real_ else min(as.numeric(st_distance(st_geometry(stations)[i], own)))
  })) %>% st_drop_geometry()

rochor_latlon <- station_points %>% filter(STN_NO == "DT13") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3414)

tibble(stations_matched_to_exits = sum(!is.na(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m)),
       median_m = median(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, na.rm = TRUE),
       p95_m = quantile(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
       rochor_adopted_m = exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m[exit_check$stn_code == "DT13"],
       rochor_latlon_m = min(as.numeric(st_distance(rochor_latlon,
                                                    exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == "ROCHOR", ]))))
```

`r sum(!is.na(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m))` of the 164 stations match their exits by name, and the adopted point lies a median of `r fmt(median(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m, na.rm = TRUE))` m from its nearest exit. Rochor's adopted `X`/`Y` point is `r fmt(exit_check$nearest_own_exit_m[exit_check$stn_code == "DT13"])` m from an exit, while its latitude/longitude point would have been `r fmt(min(as.numeric(st_distance(rochor_latlon, exits_named[exits_named$stn_name == "ROCHOR", ]))))` m away. This confirms the coordinate rule above with a second, independent LTA source.

## Future stations: auditing the URA rail layer

The URA Master Plan 2025 layer contains polygons for every existing *and* planned station footprint, identified only by name. A naive approach (keep every URA name that does not match an existing station name) treats all of them as "future" stations.

```{r}
#| label: ura-audit
ura_names <- rail_2025 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(raw = NAME, ura_name = str_squish(NAME)) %>%
  distinct()

naive_new <- setdiff(ura_names$raw, stations$stn_name)

opened_after_may22 <- c("ORCHARD BOULEVARD", "GREAT WORLD", "HAVELOCK", "MAXWELL",
                        "SHENTON WAY", "GARDEN BY THE BAY", "NAPIER", "TANJONG RHU",
                        "KATONG PARK", "TANJONG KATONG", "MARINE PARADE",
                        "MARINE TERRACE", "SIGLAP", "BAYSHORE", "HUME", "PUNGGOL COAST",
                        "TECK LEE")
sentosa_express <- c("BEACH", "IMBIAH", "RESORTS WORLD")
spelling_alias  <- c("ONE NORTH" = "ONE-NORTH", "JELEPANG" = "JELAPANG")

ura_audit <- ura_names %>%
  filter(raw %in% naive_new) %>%
  mutate(category = case_when(
    ura_name %in% planned$ura_name ~ "1. JRL / CRL1 station (in scope)",
    ura_name %in% stations$stn_name |
      str_remove(ura_name, " INTERCHANGE$") %in% stations$stn_name |
      ura_name %in% names(spelling_alias) ~
      "2. Existing station under a variant name",
    ura_name %in% opened_after_may22 ~ "3. Opened after May 2022 (TEL 3–4, Hume, Punggol Coast, Teck Lee)",
    ura_name %in% sentosa_express ~ "4. Sentosa Express (not in LTA OD data)",
    TRUE ~ "5. Other future line, unopened shell or annotation code"))

ura_audit %>%
  group_by(category) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), examples = str_c(head(ura_name, 6), collapse = ", "))
```

**Mine 4:** the naive approach flags `r length(naive_new)` "future" stations, but only `r sum(ura_audit$category == "1. JRL / CRL1 station (in scope)")` of them belong to the JRL or CRL1. The rest are:

- existing stations spelt differently (trailing spaces, or the suffix "INTERCHANGE" on, for example, *Bishan Interchange*);
- stations that opened after the study month;
- the Sentosa monorail;
- stations on lines beyond 2030, plus annotation codes such as `DE1` and `NS6`.

Treating these as new stations would have placed duplicate "competitors" on top of existing stations such as Bishan and Serangoon and split their demand artificially.

The in-scope stations are taken from the official station list. Of the 36 JRL/CRL1 stations, **7 are interchanges with existing stations**: Choa Chu Kang, Boon Lay, Jurong East, Pasir Ris, Hougang, Ang Mo Kio and Bright Hill. These are not new locations; the existing station gains a line. The remaining **29 are genuinely new**, and their coordinates come from the URA station footprints.

```{r}
#| label: planned-stations
ura_points <- rail_2025 %>%
  mutate(ura_name = str_squish(NAME)) %>%
  group_by(ura_name) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry), .groups = "drop") %>%
  st_point_on_surface()

planned <- planned %>% mutate(ura_name = str_squish(ura_name))

new_stations <- planned %>%
  filter(is.na(interchange_with)) %>%
  left_join(ura_points, by = "ura_name") %>%
  st_as_sf() %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name, line)

interchange_upgrades <- planned %>% filter(!is.na(interchange_with))

stopifnot(nrow(new_stations) == 29, !any(st_is_empty(new_stations)),
          all(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with %in% stations$stn_code))

new_stations %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(line, name = "new_stations")
```

The scenario therefore compares two networks:

- **Base**: the May 2022 network of 164 stations.
- **Expanded**: the base plus 29 new JRL/CRL1 stations, with 7 existing stations upgraded to interchanges.

Stations that opened between June 2022 and 2026 (TEL 3–4, Hume, Punggol Coast, Teck Lee) are deliberately left out of both networks, so that the difference between the two networks isolates the effect of the JRL and CRL1.

## Station attributes and the rail network graph

Each station code is split into its line prefix (`NS`, `EW`, `CG`, …), and prefixes are grouped into line families (for example, `CG` belongs to the East-West Line and `CE` to the Circle Line). Two attraction variables follow:

- `n_lines`: the number of distinct line families serving the station. Interchanges score 2 or 3.
- `lrt`: TRUE for stations served only by LRT. LRT stations act as feeders inside towns and offer a lower level of service than MRT stations.

A network graph is also built by linking consecutive station numbers along each line, plus the branch and loop connections (the Changi Airport branch, the Circle Line extension and the LRT loops). Edges are weighted by straight-line length. The graph provides network distances for the SIM and a closeness-centrality candidate for the Huff attraction.

```{r}
#| label: network-functions
line_family <- function(prefix) {
  case_when(prefix %in% c("EW", "CG") ~ "EWL", prefix %in% c("CC", "CE") ~ "CCL",
            prefix == "NS" ~ "NSL", prefix == "NE" ~ "NEL", prefix == "DT" ~ "DTL",
            prefix == "TE" ~ "TEL", prefix == "BP" ~ "BPLRT",
            prefix %in% c("SE", "SW", "STC") ~ "SKLRT",
            prefix %in% c("PE", "PW", "PTC") ~ "PGLRT",
            prefix %in% c("JS", "JW", "JE") ~ "JRL", prefix == "CR" ~ "CRL")
}

explode_codes <- function(stn_tbl) {
  stn_tbl %>%
    select(stn_code) %>%
    mutate(code = str_split(stn_code, "/")) %>%
    unnest(code) %>%
    mutate(prefix = str_extract(code, "^[A-Z]+"),
           num    = as.integer(str_extract(code, "[0-9]+$")),
           family = line_family(prefix))
}

build_edges <- function(codes, xy) {
  hub <- function(code) codes$stn_code[codes$code == code]
  ends <- function(p) { x <- codes %>% filter(prefix == p) %>% arrange(num)
                        c(first(x$stn_code), last(x$stn_code)) }
  seq_edges <- codes %>% filter(!is.na(num)) %>% arrange(prefix, num) %>%
    group_by(prefix) %>% mutate(to = lead(stn_code)) %>% ungroup() %>%
    filter(!is.na(to)) %>% transmute(from = stn_code, to)
  links <- bind_rows(
    tibble(from = hub("EW4"),  to = hub("CG1")),       # Changi Airport branch
    tibble(from = hub("CC4"),  to = hub("CE1")),       # Circle Line extension
    tibble(from = hub("BP13"), to = hub("BP6")),       # Bukit Panjang LRT loop
    tibble(from = hub("STC"),  to = c(ends("SE"), ends("SW"))),   # Sengkang LRT loops
    tibble(from = hub("PTC"),  to = c(ends("PE"), ends("PW"))))   # Punggol LRT loops
  if (any(codes$prefix == "JE")) links <- bind_rows(links,
    tibble(from = hub("JS3"), to = hub("JE1")),        # JRL East branch at Tengah
    tibble(from = hub("JS7"), to = hub("JW1")))        # JRL West branch at Bahar Junction
  bind_rows(seq_edges, links) %>% distinct() %>%
    mutate(w_km = sqrt(rowSums((xy[from, ] - xy[to, ])^2)) / 1000)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: network-base
codes_base <- explode_codes(st_drop_geometry(stations))
xy_base <- st_coordinates(stations); rownames(xy_base) <- stations$stn_code
edges_base <- build_edges(codes_base, xy_base)
g_base <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_base, directed = FALSE, vertices = stations$stn_code)

station_attr <- codes_base %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(n_lines = n_distinct(family), lrt = all(str_detect(family, "LRT")), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(closeness = closeness(g_base, weights = edges_base$w_km, normalized = TRUE)[stn_code])

c(connected = is_connected(g_base), nodes = vcount(g_base), edges = ecount(g_base))
station_attr %>% count(n_lines, lrt)
```

The graph is connected (164 nodes). There are 137 single-line stations, 26 two-line interchanges and one three-line interchange (Dhoby Ghaut), and 37 stations are LRT-only.

The expanded network reuses the same functions. Each JRL/CRL1 code is attached to its interchange station, or added as a new node, and the two JRL branches are linked at Tengah and Bahar Junction.

```{r}
#| label: network-expanded
stations_exp <- bind_rows(
  stations %>% mutate(status = "Existing"),
  new_stations %>% transmute(stn_code, stn_name, status = "New (JRL/CRL1)"))

codes_exp <- bind_rows(
  codes_base,
  planned %>% transmute(code = stn_code, stn_code = coalesce(interchange_with, stn_code)) %>%
    mutate(prefix = str_extract(code, "^[A-Z]+"), num = as.integer(str_extract(code, "[0-9]+$")),
           family = line_family(prefix)))

xy_exp <- st_coordinates(stations_exp); rownames(xy_exp) <- stations_exp$stn_code
edges_exp <- build_edges(codes_exp, xy_exp)
g_exp <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_exp, directed = FALSE, vertices = stations_exp$stn_code)

station_attr_exp <- codes_exp %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(n_lines = n_distinct(family), lrt = all(str_detect(family, "LRT")), .groups = "drop")

stations_exp <- stations_exp %>% left_join(station_attr_exp, by = "stn_code")
c(connected = is_connected(g_exp), nodes = vcount(g_exp),
  upgraded_interchanges = sum(station_attr_exp$n_lines[match(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with,
                                                       station_attr_exp$stn_code)] >
                              station_attr$n_lines[match(interchange_upgrades$interchange_with,
                                                         station_attr$stn_code)]))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-network
#| fig-cap: "The rail network graph used in the analysis. Grey lines and dots show the May 2022 network; orange shows the JRL and CRL Phase 1 links and the 29 new stations."
#| fig-height: 6.5
edge_lines <- function(edges, xy) {
  st_sfc(pmap(list(edges$from, edges$to),
              \(a, b) st_linestring(rbind(xy[a, ], xy[b, ]))), crs = 3414) %>%
    st_sf(geometry = .)
}
net_base_sf <- edge_lines(edges_base, xy_exp)
net_new_sf  <- edge_lines(anti_join(edges_exp, edges_base, by = c("from", "to")), xy_exp)

tm_shape(subzones) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey85", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(net_base_sf) + tm_lines(col = "grey45", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_shape(net_new_sf) + tm_lines(col = "#d95f02", lwd = 2.2) +
  tm_shape(stations) + tm_dots(fill = "grey30", size = 0.12) +
  tm_shape(new_stations) + tm_dots(fill = "#d95f02", size = 0.25) +
  tm_shape(new_stations %>% filter(stn_code %in% c("JS3", "JW3", "JE7", "CR2", "CR10"))) +
  tm_text("stn_name", size = 0.55, ymod = 0.7, col = "#a63f00") +
  tm_title("Base network (May 2022) and JRL / CRL1 extensions") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
```

The JRL fills the large rail gap in the Jurong–Tengah–NTU area, which the existing EWL serves only along its southern edge. CRL1 adds an orbital link through Pasir Ris, Tampines North, Hougang and Ang Mo Kio. It crosses all four radial lines and so offers a north-eastern bypass of the congested city centre. The map makes the first planning question obvious: the JRL serves some of the emptiest land in the dataset (Tengah, the Jurong industrial belt), whereas CRL1 cuts through mature, dense towns.

## Origins: resident market potential

```{r}
#| label: population-clean
pop <- pop_raw %>%
  filter(Number != "Total", !str_detect(str_to_upper(Number), "- ?TOTAL$")) %>%
  transmute(SUBZONE_N = str_to_upper(str_squish(Number)),
            pop = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Total_Total)))

tibble(subzone_rows = nrow(pop),
       dash_values_coded_zero = sum(is.na(pop$pop)),
       unmatched_in_boundary = length(setdiff(pop$SUBZONE_N, str_to_upper(subzones$SUBZONE_N))),
       total_residents = sum(pop$pop, na.rm = TRUE))
```

**Mine 5:** the Census table mixes planning-area subtotal rows ("Ang Mo Kio - Total") with subzone rows, and one subtotal uses a different spelling ("CHANGI- TOTAL"). It also codes nil population as "-". Both kinds of subtotal are removed with a pattern that tolerates the missing space. A "-" is converted to 0, not to NA, because SingStat uses it for "nil". After cleaning, every Census subzone matches a boundary polygon, and the total of 4,044,210 residents (rounding aside) matches the published national figure.

A centroid is a poor proxy for where people actually live in large subzones that are mostly industrial land, parkland or reservoir. **Population-weighted centroids** are therefore computed as the footprint-area-weighted mean location of HDB blocks within each subzone. Subzones without HDB blocks (landed or condominium estates) fall back to `st_point_on_surface()`.

```{r}
#| label: origins
hdb_pt <- hdb %>%
  mutate(area_m2 = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_point_on_surface() %>%
  select(area_m2)

hdb_centroids <- hdb_pt %>%
  st_join(subzones %>% select(SUBZONE_N)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(SUBZONE_N)) %>%
  mutate(x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1], y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(SUBZONE_N) %>%
  summarise(cx = weighted.mean(x, area_m2), cy = weighted.mean(y, area_m2),
            hdb_blocks = n(), .groups = "drop")

make_origins <- function(sz) {
  pos <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(sz)))
  sz %>%
    left_join(hdb_centroids, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
    mutate(ox = coalesce(cx, pos[, 1]), oy = coalesce(cy, pos[, 2]),
           centroid = if_else(is.na(cx), "Point on surface", "HDB-weighted"))
}

origins_poly <- subzones %>%
  left_join(pop, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(pop = replace_na(pop, 0)) %>%
  filter(pop > 0) %>%
  make_origins() %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N, pop, ox, oy, centroid)

origins_pt <- origins_poly %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("ox", "oy"), crs = 3414)

origins_poly %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(centroid) %>% summarise(subzones = n(), residents = sum(pop))
```

## Observed station demand and destination attributes

The dependent variable is **weekday morning-peak (06:00–09:59) tap-ins** at each station, summed over May 2022. This choice follows Chapter 15's morning-peak convention and fits the Huff logic. Morning-peak boardings are overwhelmingly home-based, so they are the trips generated by resident population. Total daily ridership (tap-ins plus tap-outs) also counts trips *attracted* by jobs and malls, which no residential model can explain. Total ridership is kept as a secondary measure for context.

Several station attributes are also derived for each of the 193 stations, using catchments of roughly a 10-minute walk (800 m) or a 5-minute walk (400 m):

- **HDB footprint within 800 m**: residential intensity;
- **job, education and residential floor area within 800 m**, from the Master Plan land use (parcel area × gross plot ratio). Because the Master Plan records *planned* land use, it already contains the Jurong Innovation District and the Tengah town, which is exactly what is needed to describe stations that do not exist yet;
- **bus stops within 400 m**: the number of LTA bus stops within 400 m, a measure of feeder-bus access;
- **OSM points of interest within 800 m**, grouped into food & retail, education, health, and leisure & civic destinations (@sec-va-mci).

```{r}
#| label: destinations
am_peak <- od_raw %>% filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", between(TIME_PER_HOUR, 6, 9))

demand <- stations %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(stn_code) %>%
  left_join(am_peak %>% count(stn_code = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "am_tapin"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(od_raw %>% count(stn_code = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "all_tapin"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(od_raw %>% count(stn_code = DESTINATION_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "all_tapout"),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(total_ridership = all_tapin + all_tapout)

hdb800 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800), hdb_pt) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>%
  summarise(hdb_ha_800m = sum(area_m2, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e4, .groups = "drop")

weekdays_may22 <- 19   # 22 Mon–Fri minus Labour Day (2 May), Hari Raya Puasa (3 May), Vesak (16 May)

# Land-use attractors within 800 m: floor area = parcel area x gross plot ratio (GPR).
# GPR is "EVA" (subject to evaluation) or missing for some parcels; these count at GPR = 1.
lu_typed <- landuse %>%
  mutate(gpr_num = coalesce(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(GPR)), 1),
         type = case_when(str_detect(LU_DESC, "BUSINESS|COMMERCIAL|WHITE|HOTEL|HEALTH") ~ "job_ha",
                          LU_DESC == "EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTION" ~ "edu_ha",
                          TRUE ~ "res_ha"))

lu_800 <- st_intersection(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800),
                          lu_typed %>% select(type, gpr_num)) %>%
  mutate(floor_ha = as.numeric(st_area(.)) * if_else(type == "edu_ha", 1, gpr_num) / 1e4) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code, type) %>% summarise(floor_ha = sum(floor_ha), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = floor_ha, values_fill = 0)

bus_400 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 400),
                   bus_stops %>% select(BUS_STOP_N)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(stn_code) %>% summarise(bus_stops_400m = sum(!is.na(BUS_STOP_N)), .groups = "drop")

# OSM points of interest within 800 m, grouped with Geofabrik's thematic code ranges
# (23xx catering, 25xx shops, 26xx money; 21xx health; 20xx/22xx/27xx public, leisure, tourism).
# Street furniture (benches, bins, vending machines, 29xx) is excluded.
poi_grouped <- osm_poi %>%
  mutate(group = case_when(
    code %/% 100 %in% c(23, 25, 26) ~ "poi_food_retail",
    fclass %in% c("school", "university", "college", "kindergarten") ~ "poi_edu",
    code %/% 100 == 21 ~ "poi_health",
    code %/% 100 %in% c(20, 22, 27) ~ "poi_leisure_civic")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group))

poi_800 <- st_join(st_buffer(stations_exp %>% select(stn_code), 800), poi_grouped %>% select(group)) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  count(stn_code, group) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

attractors <- stations_exp %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(stn_code) %>%
  left_join(lu_800, by = "stn_code") %>% left_join(bus_400, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(poi_800, by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(across(-stn_code, \(x) replace_na(x, 0)))

summary(demand %>% select(am_tapin, total_ridership))
count(st_drop_geometry(poi_grouped), group)
summary(attractors %>% select(-stn_code))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-observed
#| fig-cap: "Observed weekday morning-peak tap-ins (May 2022) over resident population density. Large symbols sit in the dense HDB towns at the ends of the radial lines, not in the CBD."
#| fig-height: 6.5
pop_density <- subzones %>%
  left_join(pop, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(density = replace_na(pop, 0) / (as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6))

obs_map <- stations %>% left_join(demand, by = "stn_code")

tm_shape(pop_density) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "density",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fixed",
                                              breaks = c(0, 1, 5000, 15000, 30000, 60000),
                                              values = "brewer.greys"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residents per km²"),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.2) +
  tm_shape(obs_map) +
  tm_symbols(size = "am_tapin", fill = "#176b87", col = "white", fill_alpha = 0.8,
             size.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values.scale = 1.2),
             size.legend = tm_legend(title = "AM-peak tap-ins (month)")) +
  tm_title("Where Singapore boards the train in the morning") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: top-am
#| include: false
top_am <- demand %>% left_join(st_drop_geometry(stations), by = "stn_code") %>%
  slice_max(am_tapin, n = 6)
rp_rank <- rank(-demand$am_tapin)[demand$stn_code == "EW14/NS26"]
```

Morning boardings concentrate in the dense HDB towns of the north and west. The six busiest stations are `r str_c(str_to_title(top_am$stn_name), collapse = ", ")`, led by `r str_to_title(top_am$stn_name[1])` with `r fmt(top_am$am_tapin[1])` morning tap-ins in the month. By contrast, Raffles Place, the CBD's busiest *destination*, ranks only `r rp_rank`th of 164 for morning boardings. The same pattern confirms why the model is calibrated on morning tap-ins: the spatial distribution follows where residents live, which is exactly the process the Huff model represents. LRT stations (the small symbols inside Sengkang, Punggol and Bukit Panjang) board noticeably fewer riders than nearby MRT hubs of similar catchment, because many residents bypass the LRT and travel straight to the hub.

```{r}
#| label: fig-desire
#| fig-cap: "Desire lines of the 60 largest station-to-station morning-peak flows (line width proportional to trips)."
#| fig-height: 6.5
top_flows <- am_peak %>%
  count(orig = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, dest = DESTINATION_PT_CODE, wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "trips") %>%
  filter(orig != dest) %>%
  slice_max(trips, n = 60)

flow_sf <- top_flows %>%
  mutate(geometry = st_sfc(map2(orig, dest, \(a, b) st_linestring(rbind(xy_base[a, ], xy_base[b, ]))),
                           crs = 3414)) %>%
  st_as_sf()

tm_shape(subzones) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey85", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(net_base_sf) + tm_lines(col = "grey80", lwd = 0.8) +
  tm_shape(flow_sf) +
  tm_lines(lwd = "trips", col = "#176b87", col_alpha = 0.6,
           lwd.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values.scale = 6),
           lwd.legend = tm_legend(title = "AM-peak trips (month)")) +
  tm_title("The 60 heaviest morning flows") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

The heaviest morning flows are not radial commutes into the CBD. They are **short movements into regional centres and employment nodes**:

- Choa Chu Kang, Boon Lay, Yew Tee and Bukit Batok into the Jurong East regional centre;
- Lakeside, Boon Lay and Pioneer into Joo Koon, the gateway to the Jurong and Tuas industrial estates;
- Pasir Ris into Tampines;
- Ang Mo Kio, Toa Payoh and Newton into Novena, Singapore's medical hub.

Rail serves regional-centre trips as much as city-bound ones. It also means that where people *board* is shaped by short-range competition between neighbouring stations, which is the process the Huff model represents.

# Spatial interaction data frames {#sec-sidf}

This section builds the four data frames required by Tasks 1–3. The origin and destination identifiers share column names (`SUBZONE_N`, `stn_code`) across all of them so that they join without renaming.

```{r}
#| label: sidf
origin_df <- origins_pt %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, REGION_N, market_potential = pop, centroid)

destination_df <- stations_exp %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(stn_code, stn_name, status, n_lines_2030 = n_lines, lrt) %>%
  left_join(station_attr %>% select(stn_code, n_lines, closeness), by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(hdb800, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(attractors, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(demand %>% select(stn_code, observed_am_tapin = am_tapin, total_ridership),
            by = "stn_code")

dist_long <- function(o_pt, s_pt) {
  D <- st_distance(o_pt, s_pt) %>% units::drop_units()
  dimnames(D) <- list(o_pt$SUBZONE_N, s_pt$stn_code)
  as_tibble(D, rownames = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
    pivot_longer(-SUBZONE_N, names_to = "stn_code", values_to = "dist_m") %>%
    mutate(dist_km = pmax(dist_m, 100) / 1000)          # 100 m floor avoids d = 0
}

si_existing <- dist_long(origins_pt, stations) %>%
  left_join(origin_df %>% select(SUBZONE_N, market_potential), by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  left_join(destination_df %>% select(stn_code, n_lines, lrt, observed_am_tapin), by = "stn_code")

si_expanded <- dist_long(origins_pt, stations_exp) %>%
  left_join(origin_df %>% select(SUBZONE_N, market_potential), by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  left_join(destination_df %>% select(stn_code, status, n_lines = n_lines_2030, lrt), by = "stn_code")

tibble(data_frame = c("origin_df", "destination_df", "si_existing", "si_expanded"),
       rows = c(nrow(origin_df), nrow(destination_df), nrow(si_existing), nrow(si_expanded)),
       key_columns = c("SUBZONE_N, market_potential",
                       "stn_code, observed_am_tapin, n_lines (2022), n_lines_2030, lrt, hdb_ha_800m, job/edu/res floor area, bus services, closeness",
                       "SUBZONE_N, stn_code, dist_km, market_potential, n_lines, lrt",
                       "SUBZONE_N, stn_code, dist_km, market_potential, n_lines, lrt, status"))
```

`si_existing` has 286 origins × 164 stations = `r fmt(nrow(si_existing))` rows, and `si_expanded` has 286 × 193 = `r fmt(nrow(si_expanded))` rows. Distances are straight-line distances from population-weighted centroids, with a 100 m floor so that the power function $d^{-\lambda}$ stays finite.

# Station-to-station spatial interaction models {#sec-sim}

## Flow data and distance measure

Following Chapter 16, intra-station pairs (tap-in and tap-out at the same station) are excluded, and every remaining origin–destination pair is kept, including zero-flow pairs, so that the model also has to explain *absent* links. Two distance measures are compared:

- straight-line distance;
- **network distance**: the shortest path along the rail graph, which is closer to what passengers actually travel. Two stations either side of a river may be close in a straight line but far apart by rail.

```{r}
#| label: sim-data
net_dist <- distances(g_base, weights = edges_base$w_km)
euc_dist <- st_distance(stations) %>% units::drop_units() / 1000
dimnames(euc_dist) <- list(stations$stn_code, stations$stn_code)

sim_data <- expand_grid(orig = stations$stn_code, dest = stations$stn_code) %>%
  filter(orig != dest) %>%
  left_join(am_peak %>% count(orig = ORIGIN_PT_CODE, dest = DESTINATION_PT_CODE,
                              wt = TOTAL_TRIPS, name = "trips"), by = c("orig", "dest")) %>%
  mutate(trips = replace_na(trips, 0),
         euc_km = euc_dist[cbind(orig, dest)],
         net_km = net_dist[cbind(orig, dest)]) %>%
  left_join(hdb800 %>% transmute(orig = stn_code, o_hdb = pmax(hdb_ha_800m, 0.99)), by = "orig") %>%
  left_join(station_attr %>% transmute(dest = stn_code, d_lines = n_lines,
                                       d_lrt = as.numeric(lrt)), by = "dest")

tibble(pairs = nrow(sim_data), zero_pairs = pct(mean(sim_data$trips == 0)),
       total_trips = fmt(sum(sim_data$trips)),
       corr_euclid_network = round(cor(sim_data$euc_km, sim_data$net_km), 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-distance-choice
dbc_euc <- glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(euc_km), family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data)
dbc_net <- glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(net_km), family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data)

CalcRSquared <- function(observed, estimated) cor(observed, estimated)^2

tibble(distance = c("Euclidean", "Network"),
       beta_distance = c(coef(dbc_euc)["log(euc_km)"], coef(dbc_net)["log(net_km)"]),
       AIC = c(AIC(dbc_euc), AIC(dbc_net)),
       R2 = c(CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(dbc_euc)),
              CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(dbc_net))))
```

Network distance gives the lower AIC and the higher R², so it is used for the SIM family below.

## Calibrating the four SIMs

The origin attribute is residential intensity (HDB footprint within 800 m, a proxy for the people who can walk to the station). The destination attributes are service level (`d_lines`) and LRT status. These are the station-level analogues of the age-band population variables used in Chapter 16.

```{r}
#| label: sim-models
sim_models <- list(
  unconstrained = glm(trips ~ log(o_hdb) + log(d_lines) + d_lrt + log(net_km),
                      family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  origin_constrained = glm(trips ~ orig + log(d_lines) + d_lrt + log(net_km),
                           family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  destination_constrained = glm(trips ~ dest + log(o_hdb) + log(net_km),
                                family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data),
  doubly_constrained = glm(trips ~ orig + dest + log(net_km),
                           family = poisson(link = "log"), data = sim_data))

sim_summary <- imap_dfr(sim_models, \(m, nm) tibble(
  model = nm,
  beta_distance = coef(m)["log(net_km)"],
  beta_origin_hdb = coef(m)["log(o_hdb)"],
  beta_dest_lines = coef(m)["log(d_lines)"],
  beta_dest_lrt = coef(m)["d_lrt"],
  R2 = CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(m)),
  RMSE = sqrt(mean((sim_data$trips - fitted(m))^2))))

sim_summary %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
compare_performance(sim_models, metrics = "RMSE")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed versus fitted station-to-station flows for the four SIMs (log scales; the dashed line is perfect fit)."
#| fig-height: 7
sim_fit <- imap(sim_models, \(m, nm) {
  tibble(obs = sim_data$trips, fit = fitted(m)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(fit + 1, obs + 1)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.5, colour = "#176b87") +
    geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
    labs(title = str_replace(nm, "_", " "),
         subtitle = str_c("R² = ", round(CalcRSquared(sim_data$trips, fitted(m)), 3)),
         x = "Fitted trips + 1", y = "Observed trips + 1") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
})
ggarrange(plotlist = sim_fit, ncol = 2, nrow = 2)
```

## Interpretation

```{r}
#| label: sim-numbers
#| include: false
b_dbc <- sim_summary$beta_distance[sim_summary$model == "doubly_constrained"]
r2_dbc <- sim_summary$R2[sim_summary$model == "doubly_constrained"]
r2_unc <- sim_summary$R2[sim_summary$model == "unconstrained"]
```

- **Constraints matter most.** Fit rises from R² = `r round(r2_unc, 2)` (unconstrained) to `r round(r2_dbc, 2)` (doubly constrained). Station-specific origin and destination effects therefore explain far more of the flow pattern than the few attributes we can measure. Unmeasured destination pull from employment, schools and malls is the main omitted factor, which the destination fixed effects absorb.
- **Distance decay is modest.** In the doubly constrained model, a 1% increase in network distance reduces expected flow by about `r round(abs(b_dbc), 2)`%. Rail is used for long, cross-island trips; this elasticity is far weaker than the access-distance decay in the Huff model below, because people choose a *station* within walking or feeder range but will ride that station's line across the island.
- **LRT destinations attract fewer trips** (negative `d_lrt`), and **more lines attract more trips** (positive `d_lines`). Both signs agree with the Huff calibration in @sec-huff, which is reassuring.
- **Limitations.** The doubly constrained model cannot predict flows for a station with no history, because it needs a fixed effect for every origin and destination. This is why it serves as the *explanatory* benchmark, and the Huff model is used for the *predictive* step. The Poisson models also assume equidispersion. With 15% zero pairs and heavy-tailed counts the flows are overdispersed, so standard errors are too small and coefficients should be read as effect sizes, not tested for significance.

# Huff model of station choice {#sec-huff}

## Model set-up

The Huff model allocates each subzone's residents across the stations they could board at. All 164 stations are in every subzone's choice set, and the distance-decay term pushes the probability of far-away stations towards zero. The system trip rate $k$ is fixed so that predicted boardings sum to observed boardings:

$$k = \frac{\sum_j B_j^{obs}}{\sum_i Pop_i}$$

The trip rate is fixed so that calibration only has to explain the **spatial allocation** of demand. Two distance-decay functions are considered, both supported by `MCI::huff.shares()`:

- the **power** function $f(d)=d^{-\lambda}$ (the Chapter 18 default);
- the **exponential** function $f(d)=e^{-\lambda d}$.

A fast matrix implementation is used inside the optimiser. The final model is re-estimated with `MCI::huff.shares()` and `MCI::shares.total()`, exactly as in Chapter 18, and the two implementations are checked to agree.

```{r}
#| label: huff-setup
dmat <- function(o_pt, s_pt) {
  D <- st_distance(o_pt, s_pt) %>% units::drop_units()
  pmax(D, 100) / 1000
}

D_base <- dmat(origins_pt, stations)
dest_base <- destination_df %>% filter(status == "Existing") %>%
  slice(match(stations$stn_code, stn_code))
y_obs <- dest_base$observed_am_tapin
pop_i <- origins_pt$pop
k_rate <- sum(y_obs) / sum(pop_i)

decay_term <- function(D, decay) if (decay == "exp") D else log(D)

huff_general <- function(par, X, D, pop, decay = "exp", k = k_rate) {
  lambda <- par[length(par)]
  logA <- as.numeric(X %*% par[-length(par)])
  U <- exp(sweep(-lambda * decay_term(D, decay), 2, logA, "+"))
  as.numeric(k * colSums(U / rowSums(U) * pop))
}

huff_predict <- function(gamma, delta, lambda, n_lines, lrt, D, pop, decay = "exp", k = k_rate) {
  huff_general(c(gamma, delta, lambda), cbind(log(n_lines), as.numeric(lrt)), D, pop, decay, k)
}

fit_stats <- function(obs, pred) tibble(
  RMSE = sqrt(mean((obs - pred)^2)), MAE = mean(abs(obs - pred)),
  R2 = cor(obs, pred)^2)

c(trip_rate_k = round(k_rate, 3), observed_total = fmt(sum(y_obs)))
```

## Reference (null) models

A calibrated model is only useful if it beats simpler alternatives. Two reference models are evaluated:

- **R0, nearest station (all-or-nothing).** Every resident boards at the nearest station. This is the Thiessen-polygon logic often used for catchments.
- **R1, Chapter 18 default Huff.** Every station is equally attractive ($A_j=1$), with power decay and $\lambda = 2$, estimated with `MCI::huff.shares()`.

```{r}
#| label: huff-reference
nearest <- apply(D_base, 1, which.min)
pred_r0 <- as.numeric(k_rate * tapply(pop_i, factor(nearest, levels = seq_len(ncol(D_base))), sum))
pred_r0[is.na(pred_r0)] <- 0

im_r1 <- si_existing %>% transmute(SUBZONE_N, stn_code, A = 1, dist_km) %>% as.data.frame()
shares_r1 <- huff.shares(im_r1, "SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "A", "dist_km",
                         gamma = 1, lambda = -2, check_df = FALSE)
total_r1 <- shares_r1 %>%
  left_join(origin_df %>% select(SUBZONE_N, market_potential), by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  shares.total("SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "p_ij", "market_potential", check_df = FALSE)
pred_r1 <- k_rate * total_r1$sum_E_j[match(stations$stn_code, total_r1$suppliers_single)]

bind_rows(fit_stats(y_obs, pred_r0) %>% mutate(model = "R0 nearest station"),
          fit_stats(y_obs, pred_r1) %>% mutate(model = "R1 Huff, A = 1, power λ = 2")) %>%
  relocate(model)
```

The nearest-station rule explains under half of the variation. It gives every resident to one station and ignores that people regularly walk or take a feeder bus past a closer station to reach a better-served one. The default Huff model does only slightly better because it still treats an LRT halt and a three-line interchange as equally attractive.

## Calibration and model selection

Parameters are calibrated by minimising RMSE with `optim()` (Nelder–Mead, restarted from the previous optimum to confirm convergence). Model selection proceeds in two steps.

**Step 1: the distance-decay function.** With a common attraction specification (lines + LRT), the power and exponential functions are compared.

```{r}
#| label: huff-decay
X_specs <- list(
  "1 Lines"                   = cbind(log(dest_base$n_lines)),
  "2 Lines + LRT"             = cbind(log(dest_base$n_lines), dest_base$lrt),
  "3 Lines + LRT + closeness" = cbind(log(dest_base$n_lines), dest_base$lrt,
                                      log(dest_base$closeness / median(dest_base$closeness))),
  "4 Lines + LRT + HDB 800m"  = cbind(log(dest_base$n_lines), dest_base$lrt,
                                      log(pmax(dest_base$hdb_ha_800m, 0.5) / 10)),
  "5 Lines + LRT + bus stops 400m" = cbind(log(dest_base$n_lines), dest_base$lrt,
                                      log(dest_base$bus_stops_400m + 1)))

calibrate <- function(X, decay = "exp", D = D_base, pop = pop_i, y = y_obs, idx = seq_along(y)) {
  loss <- function(p) sqrt(mean((y[idx] - huff_general(p, X, D, pop, decay)[idx])^2))
  o <- optim(c(rep(0.5, ncol(X)), 2), loss, control = list(maxit = 4000))
  optim(o$par, loss, control = list(maxit = 4000))
}

decay_fits <- map(c(power = "pow", exponential = "exp"), \(dc) calibrate(X_specs[[2]], dc))

decay_table <- imap_dfr(decay_fits, \(o, nm)
  fit_stats(y_obs, huff_general(o$par, X_specs[[2]], D_base, pop_i,
                                if (nm == "power") "pow" else "exp")) %>%
    mutate(decay = nm, gamma = o$par[1], delta = o$par[2], lambda = o$par[3])) %>%
  relocate(decay)
decay_table %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-decay
#| fig-cap: "Calibrated distance-decay curves. Both are scaled to 1 at 100 m; the exponential curve drops faster beyond walking range and has a much thinner long tail."
#| fig-height: 3.8
tibble(d = seq(0.1, 6, 0.02)) %>%
  mutate(power = (d / 0.1)^(-decay_table$lambda[1]),
         exponential = exp(-decay_table$lambda[2] * (d - 0.1))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-d, names_to = "decay", values_to = "weight") %>%
  ggplot(aes(d, weight, colour = decay)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.0001)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(power = "grey50", exponential = "#176b87")) +
  labs(x = "Distance from subzone to station (km)", y = "Relative attractiveness (log)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The exponential function fits clearly better, with R² `r round(decay_table$R2[2], 3)` against `r round(decay_table$R2[1], 3)` and an RMSE lower by about `r fmt(decay_table$RMSE[1] - decay_table$RMSE[2])` boardings. @fig-decay shows why. The power function keeps a long tail, so a station 5 km away still receives a small but non-trivial share of every subzone's residents. That is unrealistic for station *access*, which is made on foot or by short feeder bus. The exponential function drops off quickly beyond walking range. This choice also matters for the scenario: with a long-tailed power function, every new station would draw small amounts of demand from stations across the island, and impacts would be spread unrealistically thin.

**Step 2: the attraction specification**, under exponential decay. Five candidates add one driver of station attractiveness at a time: lines served, the LRT-only penalty, network closeness centrality, residential intensity (HDB footprint within 800 m), and feeder-bus access (bus stops within 400 m).

```{r}
#| label: huff-calibration
calib <- map(X_specs, calibrate)

spec_table <- imap_dfr(calib, \(o, nm) {
  pred <- huff_general(o$par, X_specs[[nm]], D_base, pop_i)
  fit_stats(y_obs, pred) %>%
    mutate(spec = nm, parameters = length(o$par),
           estimates = str_c(round(o$par, 2), collapse = " / "))
}) %>% relocate(spec, parameters, estimates)
spec_table
```

```{r}
#| label: huff-choose
#| include: false
par_final <- calib[["2 Lines + LRT"]]$par
gamma_hat <- par_final[1]; delta_hat <- par_final[2]; lambda_hat <- par_final[3]
r2_final <- spec_table$R2[2]; r2_r0 <- fit_stats(y_obs, pred_r0)$R2; r2_r1 <- fit_stats(y_obs, pred_r1)$R2
r2_gain_clo <- spec_table$R2[3] - spec_table$R2[2]
r2_gain_hdb <- spec_table$R2[4] - spec_table$R2[2]
r2_gain_bus <- spec_table$R2[5] - spec_table$R2[2]
```

Specification 2 (**Lines + LRT, exponential decay**) is selected:

- It raises R² from `r round(r2_r1, 2)` (default Huff) and `r round(r2_r0, 2)` (nearest station) to `r round(r2_final, 3)`.
- **Closeness centrality** adds `r sprintf("%+.3f", r2_gain_clo)` to R². That is negligible, so it is dropped.
- **HDB floor area within 800 m** adds `r sprintf("%+.3f", r2_gain_hdb)` to R². It is still not adopted, for two reasons. It counts the same residents twice, since they are already in the origin populations. And it would systematically penalise new stations whose surrounding housing is not yet built, such as Tengah, which is exactly where the forecast matters most.
- **Bus stops within 400 m** add only `r sprintf("%+.3f", r2_gain_bus)`. This is an informative negative result. Almost every station in Singapore is surrounded by bus stops, so the *number* of nearby stops does not separate stations whose feeder services pull residents from far away (Woodlands, Boon Lay) from the rest. What matters is *where* those buses come from, which a stop count cannot capture.
- All three parameters are plausible and stable across specifications:
  - $\hat\gamma =$ `r round(gamma_hat, 2)`: a two-line interchange is about $2^{\hat\gamma} \approx$ `r round(2^gamma_hat, 1)` times as attractive as a single-line station.
  - $\hat\delta =$ `r round(delta_hat, 2)`: an LRT-only station is about $e^{\hat\delta} \approx$ `r round(exp(delta_hat), 2)` times as attractive as an MRT station, so most LRT-area residents are drawn to the town's MRT hub.
  - $\hat\lambda =$ `r round(lambda_hat, 2)` per km: every additional 500 m to a station cuts its attractiveness by about `r pct(1 - exp(-lambda_hat / 2), 0)`. This is a steep access decay, consistent with walking and short feeder trips.

```{r}
#| label: fig-surface
#| fig-cap: "Calibration surface: RMSE over the attraction exponent γ and the exponential distance-decay rate λ, holding the LRT penalty δ at its optimum. The cross marks the calibrated solution."
#| fig-height: 5
surface <- expand_grid(gamma = seq(0, 2.5, 0.1), lambda = seq(0.5, 4, 0.1)) %>%
  mutate(rmse = map2_dbl(gamma, lambda, \(g, l)
    sqrt(mean((y_obs - huff_predict(g, delta_hat, l, dest_base$n_lines, dest_base$lrt,
                                    D_base, pop_i))^2))))

ggplot(surface, aes(gamma, lambda, fill = rmse / 1000)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_contour(aes(z = rmse / 1000), colour = "white", alpha = 0.5, bins = 12) +
  annotate("point", x = gamma_hat, y = lambda_hat, shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "RMSE ('000)") +
  labs(x = "Attraction exponent γ (lines)", y = "Distance-decay rate λ (per km)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The surface has a single, well-defined minimum, so the optimiser has found the global solution and not a local one. The diagonal valley shows a trade-off between the two parameters: steeper distance decay can be partly offset by stronger attraction. This is why the cross-validation below checks that the parameters are stable.

## Final model with the MCI package

```{r}
#| label: huff-final
attraction <- function(n_lines, lrt) exp(gamma_hat * log(n_lines) + delta_hat * as.numeric(lrt))

im_existing <- si_existing %>%
  mutate(A = attraction(n_lines, lrt)) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, stn_code, A, dist_km) %>% as.data.frame()

shares_base <- huff.shares(im_existing, "SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "A", "dist_km",
                           gamma = 1, lambda = -lambda_hat, dtype = "exp", check_df = FALSE)

total_base <- shares_base %>%
  left_join(origin_df %>% select(SUBZONE_N, market_potential), by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  shares.total("SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "p_ij", "market_potential", check_df = FALSE)

pred_base <- tibble(stn_code = total_base$suppliers_single,
                    pred_base = k_rate * total_base$sum_E_j)

calibrated <- dest_base %>%
  left_join(pred_base, by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(residual = observed_am_tapin - pred_base,
         pct_error = residual / observed_am_tapin)

c(max_abs_diff_vs_matrix = max(abs(calibrated$pred_base -
    huff_predict(gamma_hat, delta_hat, lambda_hat, dest_base$n_lines, dest_base$lrt,
                 D_base, pop_i)[match(calibrated$stn_code, stations$stn_code)])))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-obs-pred
#| fig-cap: "Observed versus calibrated morning-peak tap-ins for the 164 existing stations."
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggscatterstats(calibrated, x = pred_base, y = observed_am_tapin,
               xlab = "Predicted AM-peak tap-ins (month)",
               ylab = "Observed AM-peak tap-ins (month)",
               marginal = FALSE, bf.message = FALSE,
               point.args = list(alpha = 0.6, colour = "#176b87", size = 2)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey40")
```

The calibrated model tracks observed boardings across the full range: the points lie along the 1:1 line from small LRT halts to the busiest suburban hubs, with a correlation of about `r round(sqrt(r2_final), 2)`. The largest misses are systematic, not random. They are discussed with the residual map in @fig-residual-map, and their spatial clustering is tested formally in @sec-va-moran.

## Out-of-sample validation and parameter stability

Calibrating and judging fit on the same 164 stations flatters any model. Five-fold cross-validation is used instead: stations are randomly split into five groups, parameters are re-estimated on four groups, and boardings are predicted for the held-out group.

```{r}
#| label: huff-cv
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(y_obs)))
X2 <- X_specs[["2 Lines + LRT"]]   # exponential decay (default)

cv <- map_dfr(1:5, \(f) {
  o <- calibrate(X2, idx = which(folds != f))
  pred <- huff_general(o$par, X2, D_base, pop_i)
  tibble(fold = f, gamma = o$par[1], delta = o$par[2], lambda = o$par[3],
         test_R2 = cor(y_obs[folds == f], pred[folds == f])^2,
         test_RMSE = sqrt(mean((y_obs[folds == f] - pred[folds == f])^2)))
})

cv %>% mutate(across(-fold, \(x) round(x, 3)))
cv %>% summarise(across(c(gamma, delta, lambda, test_R2), list(mean = mean, sd = sd))) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Out-of-sample R² averages `r round(mean(cv$test_R2), 2)`, close to the in-sample `r round(r2_final, 2)`, so the model is not over-fitted. The parameter estimates barely move between folds ($\lambda$ ranges from `r round(min(cv$lambda), 2)` to `r round(max(cv$lambda), 2)`). The fold-to-fold range of $\lambda$ is later used as an uncertainty band for the new-station predictions.

## Where the model errs

```{r}
#| label: fig-residual-map
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the calibrated Huff model (observed minus predicted AM-peak tap-ins). Blue = model under-predicts; red = model over-predicts."
#| fig-height: 6.5
res_map <- stations %>% left_join(calibrated %>% select(stn_code, residual), by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(abs_res = abs(residual))

tm_shape(subzones) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey85", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(res_map) +
  tm_symbols(size = "abs_res", fill = "residual",
             fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "fixed",
                                             breaks = c(-2e5, -5e4, -2e4, 2e4, 5e4, 2e5),
                                             values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
             fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Residual"),
             size.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE), col = "grey30", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(res_map %>% slice_max(abs_res, n = 8)) +
  tm_text("stn_code", size = 0.55, ymod = 0.8) +
  tm_title("Huff model residuals by station") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top"), size = 1.5) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("left", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: residual-table
calibrated %>%
  slice_max(abs(residual), n = 10) %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name, observed = fmt(observed_am_tapin),
            predicted = fmt(pred_base), residual = fmt(residual))
```

The largest residuals form three geographically coherent groups.

1. **Under-prediction along the northern North-South Line**: Admiralty, Sembawang, Yew Tee, Woodlands, Kranji and Marsiling. These towns sit at the end of a long radial line with no alternative, and the stations nearest the Causeway also serve cross-border commuters arriving from Johor by bus. Those commuters are not Singapore residents, so the Census-driven model cannot see them.
2. **Under-prediction at city-fringe nodes** such as Newton, and at big bus-interchange hubs such as Ang Mo Kio and Boon Lay. Morning tap-ins here include non-residential trips (schools, hotels, bus-to-rail transfers from far beyond walking range) that a resident-population model cannot see.
3. **Over-prediction in the east**: Tampines East, Tampines West, Bedok Reservoir and Pasir Ris. Downtown Line stage 3 stations duplicate the East-West Line inside the same towns, and the east is well served by direct buses to the Tampines regional centre and the Changi employment areas, so a smaller share of residents boards rail than the model expects.

None of these is a failure of the Huff logic itself. They point to demand sources (cross-border commuters, feeder buses, competing bus services) that are not in the model. Because the groups are *regional*, their spatial clustering is tested formally in @sec-va-moran: a regional bias would carry straight into the forecasts for new stations in the same areas.

# Predicting ridership at the JRL and CRL1 stations {#sec-scenario}

## Expanded-network prediction

The calibrated parameters are applied to the expanded network. New stations are single-line MRT stations ($n_j = 1$, not LRT); the seven interchange stations gain one line. Residential population is held at Census 2020 levels and the trip rate $k$ is unchanged. The scenario therefore answers: *if today's residents faced the 2030 network, where would they board?*

```{r}
#| label: scenario-expanded
im_expanded <- si_expanded %>%
  mutate(A = attraction(n_lines, lrt)) %>%
  select(SUBZONE_N, stn_code, A, dist_km) %>% as.data.frame()

shares_exp <- huff.shares(im_expanded, "SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "A", "dist_km",
                          gamma = 1, lambda = -lambda_hat, dtype = "exp", check_df = FALSE)

total_exp <- shares_exp %>%
  left_join(origin_df %>% select(SUBZONE_N, market_potential), by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  shares.total("SUBZONE_N", "stn_code", "p_ij", "market_potential", check_df = FALSE)

D_exp <- dmat(origins_pt, stations_exp)
lambda_band <- range(cv$lambda)
band <- map(lambda_band, \(l) huff_predict(gamma_hat, delta_hat, l, stations_exp$n_lines,
                                           stations_exp$lrt, D_exp, pop_i))

scenario <- stations_exp %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(stn_code, stn_name, status, n_lines) %>%
  left_join(tibble(stn_code = total_exp$suppliers_single, pred_exp = k_rate * total_exp$sum_E_j),
            by = "stn_code") %>%
  mutate(low = pmin(band[[1]], band[[2]]), high = pmax(band[[1]], band[[2]])) %>%
  left_join(pred_base, by = "stn_code") %>%
  left_join(planned %>% select(stn_code, line), by = "stn_code")

p25_existing <- quantile(calibrated$observed_am_tapin, 0.25)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-new-stations
#| fig-cap: "Predicted weekday AM-peak tap-ins per day at the 29 new stations (Census 2020 population). Error bars show the range implied by the cross-validated λ; the dashed line marks the lower quartile (25th percentile) of existing stations' observed boardings."
#| fig-height: 7
new_pred <- scenario %>% filter(status != "Existing") %>%
  mutate(per_day = pred_exp / weekdays_may22,
         low_d = low / weekdays_may22, high_d = high / weekdays_may22)

ggplot(new_pred, aes(per_day, fct_reorder(stn_name, per_day), fill = line)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = low_d, xmax = high_d), height = 0.3, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p25_existing / weekdays_may22, linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(JRL = "#0099aa", CRL = "#97c616")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Predicted AM-peak tap-ins per weekday", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: new-station-table
new_pred %>%
  arrange(desc(pred_exp)) %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name, line,
            per_weekday = fmt(per_day), range = str_c(fmt(low_d), "–", fmt(high_d)),
            percentile_vs_existing = pct(ecdf(calibrated$observed_am_tapin)(pred_exp), 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: scenario-numbers
#| include: false
crl_mean <- mean(new_pred$per_day[new_pred$line == "CRL"])
jrl_mean <- mean(new_pred$per_day[new_pred$line == "JRL"])
n_low <- sum(new_pred$pred_exp < p25_existing)
low_names <- new_pred %>% filter(pred_exp < p25_existing) %>% arrange(pred_exp) %>% pull(stn_name)
top3 <- new_pred %>% slice_max(pred_exp, n = 3) %>% pull(stn_name)
```

Two clear messages emerge from @fig-new-stations.

- **Stations inserted into mature HDB estates lead.** `r str_to_title(top3[1])`, `r str_to_title(top3[2])` and `r str_to_title(top3[3])` top the ranking. Each is placed in an established estate that is currently beyond comfortable walking distance of an MRT line, and each would rank in the upper quarter of today's stations from day one. On average a CRL1 station attracts about `r fmt(crl_mean)` morning tap-ins per weekday, almost twice the JRL average of `r fmt(jrl_mean)`.
- **Several JRL stations would be "ghost-risk" stations on today's population.** `r n_low` of the 29 new stations fall below the lower quartile of existing stations: `r str_c(str_to_title(low_names), collapse = ", ")`. They are of three kinds:
  - stations in employment areas with few residents, namely the Jurong industrial estate (Tukang, Jurong Hill, Jurong Pier) and the Changi aviation cluster (Aviation Park);
  - the NTU campus stations, whose student and staff trips are not home-based morning boardings;
  - Tengah, a new town that had essentially no residents at the 2020 Census.

The cross-validated uncertainty bands are narrow relative to the differences between stations, so the *ranking* of new stations is robust to parameter uncertainty, even though the absolute numbers should be treated as indicative. For the employment and campus stations, a low morning *boarding* forecast does not mean low use: these stations may be busy as morning *destinations*, which this residential model does not measure. @sec-va-mci tests this directly with an MCI destination-choice model. For Tengah, the case rests on future residents, the subject of the next section.

## Sensitivity: Tengah at build-out

A model driven by today's population cannot see tomorrow's residents, which is exactly the trap of the ghost-station debate. Tengah is planned for about **42,000 homes** across five districts. At roughly 3.1 residents per home (close to the Census 2020 average household size), build-out adds about 130,000 residents. These are allocated equally to Tengah's five residential subzones (Plantation, Park, Garden, Brickland and Forest Hill), and the expanded-network model is re-run.

```{r}
#| label: scenario-tengah
tengah_res <- c("PLANTATION", "PARK", "GARDEN", "BRICKLAND", "FOREST HILL")
tengah_add <- 42000 * 3.1 / length(tengah_res)

origins_tengah <- subzones %>%
  left_join(pop, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  mutate(pop = replace_na(pop, 0) + if_else(SUBZONE_N %in% tengah_res & PLN_AREA_N == "TENGAH",
                                            tengah_add, 0)) %>%
  filter(pop > 0) %>%
  make_origins() %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("ox", "oy"), crs = 3414)

D_tengah <- dmat(origins_tengah, stations_exp)
pred_tengah <- huff_predict(gamma_hat, delta_hat, lambda_hat, stations_exp$n_lines,
                            stations_exp$lrt, D_tengah, origins_tengah$pop)

tengah_cmp <- scenario %>%
  mutate(pred_tengah = pred_tengah) %>%
  filter(stn_code %in% c("JS2", "JS3", "JS4", "JE1", "JE2", "JE3", "JS5", "NS4/BP1")) %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name,
            census_2020 = pred_exp / weekdays_may22,
            tengah_buildout = pred_tengah / weekdays_may22)
tengah_cmp %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), fmt))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-tengah
#| fig-cap: "Predicted AM-peak tap-ins per weekday at stations around Tengah under Census 2020 population and at Tengah's planned build-out."
#| fig-height: 4.5
tengah_cmp %>%
  pivot_longer(c(census_2020, tengah_buildout), names_to = "scenario", values_to = "per_day") %>%
  mutate(scenario = recode(scenario, census_2020 = "Census 2020 population",
                           tengah_buildout = "Tengah build-out (~130k residents)")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(per_day, fct_reorder(stn_name, per_day), fill = scenario)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p25_existing / weekdays_may22, linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "#0099aa")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Predicted AM-peak tap-ins per weekday", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tengah-numbers
#| include: false
tg <- tengah_cmp %>% filter(stn_code == "JS3")
tg1 <- tengah_cmp %>% filter(stn_code == "JE1")
```

At build-out, Tengah station (JS3) rises from about `r fmt(tg$census_2020)` to about `r fmt(tg$tengah_buildout)` morning tap-ins per weekday, and Tengah Plantation (JE1) from about `r fmt(tg1$census_2020)` to `r fmt(tg1$tengah_buildout)`. Tengah station thus moves from the ghost-risk zone to well above the existing-station median of `r fmt(median(calibrated$observed_am_tapin) / weekdays_may22)`, and Tengah Plantation becomes one of the busiest stations on the JRL. This is the Hume and Buangkok story in numbers: whether a JRL station is a white elephant depends almost entirely on the **timing of housing completions relative to the line's opening**. Because the model is quick to re-run, it can be used to set a completion threshold, the number of occupied homes at which opening a station becomes justified.

# Impact on existing stations {#sec-impact}

Because the trip rate is fixed, every boarding at a new station is a boarding *diverted* from an existing station. The change at each existing station measures its exposure to the new lines.

```{r}
#| label: impact
impact <- scenario %>%
  filter(status == "Existing") %>%
  mutate(change = pred_exp - pred_base, change_pct = change / pred_base,
         upgraded = stn_code %in% interchange_upgrades$interchange_with)

impact_sf <- stations %>% left_join(impact %>% select(stn_code, change, change_pct, upgraded),
                                    by = "stn_code")

bind_rows(impact %>% slice_min(change, n = 8), impact %>% slice_max(change, n = 7)) %>%
  transmute(stn_code, stn_name, upgraded,
            before = fmt(pred_base / weekdays_may22), after = fmt(pred_exp / weekdays_may22),
            change_per_day = fmt(change / weekdays_may22), change_pct = pct(change_pct))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-impact
#| fig-cap: "Interactive map: predicted change in AM-peak tap-ins at existing stations after JRL and CRL1 open. Red = losing riders to new stations; blue = gaining (mainly upgraded interchanges); grey = change under 1%. Orange lines and dots are the new JRL/CRL1 links and stations. Click a station for its figures."
impact_view <- impact_sf %>%
```
